newsitem.title: USA: Iran economy doing better, but more needed -IMF.
newsitem.headline: Iran economy doing better, but more needed -IMF.

text.p: Iran looks set to enjoy better economic times in 1996/97 despite U.S. sanctions, but it still needs to carry out tough reforms to put its economy on a sounder long-run footing, IMF officials said on Monday.
Speaking to reporters after talks with an Iranian delegation, the officials painted a picture of an economy that has weathered a debt crunch but remains fragile and too dependent on oil.

"The situation is not critical," said Antonio Furtado, the IMF division chief dealing with Iran. But "there is a great programme of reform that has still to be taken," his boss, Paul Chabrier, Director of the IMF's Middle East department, added.
The programme includes introduction of a value added tax, overhaul of Iran's foreign currency regime and an increase in heavily-subsidised prices for gasoline and petroleum products.
The International Monetary Fund is providing Tehran with technical advice, but does not have a loan deal with the country and there are no plans for one.

Chabrier said Iran's economy is expected to grow some four percent in the year ending next March, up from 3.5 percent last year and 1.6 percent the year before. Inflation is expected to fall to about 20 percent from over 50 percent.
He said he saw the current account surplus rising to about $4 billion in 1996/97, from $3.5 billion last year.
Iran, which was $11 billion in arrears to its foreign creditors as recently as March 1994, has no trouble now servicing its debt now following a series of bilateral reschedulings, Chabrier sad.

Arrears on its roughly $23 billion of foreign debt have been reduced to some $200 million, while foreign currency reserves stand at a "comfortable" $8 to $8.5 billion. Credit lines are being reinstated, he added.
Chabrier said U.S. sanctions had probably deterred some foreign investors, but other factors, including price controls and the foreign exchange regime, had been more important.

Washington imposed a trade and investment ban on Iran in 1995, accusing it of sponsoring terrorism and seeking nuclear weapons -- charges denied by Tehran. Congress followed up in August with a law aimed at punishing non-U.S. firms investing $40 million or more in a year in Iran's energy sector.
Iran was able dig its way out of its 1994 debt hole largely through a steep reduction in imports. But that is not sustainable in the long run, IMF officials believe.
"You still have a balance of payments structure that is quite fragile" and depends largely on oil and natural gas exports, Chabrier said.

To help put Iran's economy on a sounder footing, the IMF recommended that Iran unify its foreign exchange rates. It now has three rates -- an official rate of 1,750 rials to the dollar dollar, an export rate of 3,000 and a black market price of some 4,800.
Other recommendations include: more trade liberalisation, greater independence for the central bank, and banking sector reforms to allow banks to set their own deposit rates.
